title: Nehemiah 6:15–19
context: The wall is finished on the twenty-fifth day of Elul, in fifty-two days. The surrounding nations are afraid and lose confidence, recognizing that the work was done by God. Yet within Judah, nobles maintain correspondence with Tobiah, who is connected to leading families by marriage. They praise him to Nehemiah and report Nehemiah's words to him, while Tobiah continues sending letters to frighten him.

verses.text: So the wall was finished in the twenty-fifth day of Elul, in fifty-two days.
verses.arminianNotes: "So the wall was finished in the twenty-fifth day of Elul, in fifty-two days." Arminian readers see diligent, persevering work carried through to completion despite constant opposition.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the brief statement marks the triumph of the whole project. Both traditions celebrate this as shared ground: God's purpose for Jerusalem's wall is accomplished.

verses.text: When all our enemies heard of it, all the nations that were around us were afraid, and they lost their confidence; for they perceived that this work was done by our God.
verses.arminianNotes: The nations are afraid and lose confidence, "for they perceived that this work was done by our God." Arminian readers note that the people's faithful labor and God's help together bring the result.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that even the enemies recognize God's hand. Psalm 127:1 says, "Unless the LORD builds the house, they who build it labor in vain." Both traditions treat this as shared ground.

verses.text: Moreover in those days the nobles of Judah sent many letters to Tobiah, and Tobiah’s letters came to them.
verses.arminianNotes: The nobles of Judah exchange many letters with Tobiah. Arminian readers note that some leaders choose divided loyalty, maintaining ties with an enemy of the work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that opposition continues even after the wall is finished. The threat now comes through relationships within the community rather than from outside.

verses.text: For there were many in Judah sworn to him because he was the son-in-law of Shecaniah the son of Arah; and his son Jehohanan had taken the daughter of Meshullam the son of Berechiah as wife.
verses.arminianNotes: Many in Judah were sworn to Tobiah because of his marriage into Shecaniah's family and his son's marriage to Meshullam's daughter. Arminian readers note how family ties can pull loyalties in conflicting directions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that a Meshullam son of Berechiah appears among the builders in Nehemiah 3:4. The narrator records these connections without fully explaining them.

verses.text: Also they spoke of his good deeds before me, and reported my words to him. Tobiah sent letters to put me in fear.
verses.arminianNotes: They praise Tobiah's good deeds to Nehemiah and report his words to Tobiah, who sends letters "to put me in fear." Arminian readers see continuing pressure that calls for steady faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the chapter ends with the same aim the enemies have pursued throughout: to make Nehemiah afraid. God's finished work stands, even as the struggle goes on.
